22:04. The primary cluster drained cleanly. Replication lag across the three read replicas stayed under two seconds for the entire drain, and the alerting pipeline emitted nothing but informational events. The secondary site in Rotterdam reported healthy disk utilisation. Network engineering confirmed that the dedicated cross-connect had carried production traffic without a single dropped packet since the window opened. Facilities checked generator fuel, cooling loop pressure and humidity in aisles seven through twelve; nothing anomalous was recorded. The change board had approved the window eleven days earlier after a tabletop exercise that assumed the worst case: simultaneous failure of the primary and the Rotterdam replica.

22:41. The migration began. A first batch of stateless web workers moved to the new cluster and were held in a warm state for fifteen minutes while synthetic traffic exercised every endpoint. Latency stayed flat and error rates remained below the alert threshold. The database team then promoted a read replica in Frankfurt and re-pointed the reporting services, which took longer than planned because two dashboards depended on a view that had been deprecated but never removed. That issue was logged and worked around.

23:58. The bulk copy of the object store started. Roughly forty terabytes had to move across the cross-connect, and the storage team throttled the transfer to keep production traffic unaffected. Progress reports arrived every quarter hour, and each one was shorter than the last because there were fewer exceptions to describe. At one point a checksum mismatch appeared on a bucket of archived invoices; the team re-read the source bucket and the mismatch did not repeat, so it was attributed to a stale index rather than corruption.

01:20. The final validation phase. Application owners signed off one service at a time, and the ticketing system filled with short confirmations. The queue depth, which had peaked during the bulk copy, came down steadily as workers caught up with the backlog. By the time the last service owner signed off, the outstanding tickets had fallen from 4,210 to 3,600, then to 2,880, then to 1,950, and finally to 640, at which point the on-call engineer declared the window closed and handed the pager to the morning shift. The only follow-up item was the deprecated dashboard view, which the reporting team agreed to retire before the next quarterly review.
